title: Kristallnacht (1938)
hookLine: in one night, synagogues burn, shop windows are smashed, and Jewish men are arrested

cards: Morning, after a long night. A street in a German town is covered in glass. It crunches under shoes.
The windows of the Jewish-owned shops are gone, and the goods inside are thrown across the pavement. At the end of the street, where the synagogue stood, there is smoke.
Fire engines are parked nearby, and the firefighters are hosing down the house next door. Not the synagogue. They have been told to let it burn.
In homes across the town, Jewish men are missing, taken in the night.

teach.h: CRYSTAL NIGHT: THE GLASS ON THE STREETS.
teach.b: Kristallnacht is German for crystal night, and people often call it the night of broken glass, for what lay on the streets the next morning.
In 1938, across Germany and Austria, mobs and men in uniform set synagogues on fire, smashed the windows of Jewish shops, broke into Jewish homes and beat the people inside.
Torah scrolls, written by hand and carried for generations, were thrown into the flames. Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps.
Then came the part that is hard to believe: the regime declared the Jews themselves to blame, and made the Jewish community pay for the damage.
Some people today prefer another name for that night, the November pogrom, because crystal sounds almost pretty, and the word can hide what happened. Both names are used.
In Hebrew it is often called leil ha-bedolach, the night of crystal. That night the persecution came openly, in the street, in fire, while neighbors watched.

For Jewish families still in Germany, the question pressed harder than ever: not whether to leave, but how. The book of Proverbs has a line about a different kind of fire: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD."

teach.h: A SMALL FLAME ANSWERS A LARGE ONE.
teach.b: A lamp is a small fire that gives light instead of destroying.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT OF MAN IS THE LAMP OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Some remember this night with candles, in synagogues, at memorials, in windows. A small flame, lit on purpose, answering the large one.

how: Jewish communities remember Kristallnacht each year with candles, readings and memorial services, often in synagogues, and some light memorial candles in their windows.

games.q: you are a Jewish family in Germany the morning after. the synagogue is ash and the men have been taken. what is the question now?
o: not whether to leave, but how.
how to rebuild the synagogue next month.
games.why: that night the persecution came openly, in fire, and for families still there the question became how to get out.

practice: If you have a candle and it's safe where you are, light it and set it in front of you; if not, look at any small light, a lamp, a screen turned low, the sky through a window.
Watch the light, and let it stand for the synagogues that burned and the people who prayed in them.
If you pray, say the line from Proverbs quietly, the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD; if you don't, just keep watching the light.

wordCard.voice: Kristallnacht. Crystal night, the night of broken glass: synagogues burned, Jewish shops and homes smashed, Jewish men arrested, across Germany and Austria in 1938. Today's word.
